title: How commuters travel
prompt: The table shows the percentage of journeys to work made using four forms of transport in the fictional city of Westbridge in 2010 and 2020. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Write at least 150 words.

The table compares the proportions of commuting journeys made by car, bus, bicycle and on foot in Westbridge in 2010 and 2020.

Overall, cars remained the most common means of travelling to work, although their share fell substantially. Bus travel and cycling both became more popular, with cycling recording the largest increase, while the proportion of journeys made on foot stayed the same.

In 2010, cars accounted for 55% of journeys, which was more than twice the figure for buses, at 25%. By 2020, the car share had declined to 40%, a decrease of 15 percentage points. Over the same period, the proportion of trips made by bus rose by five percentage points to 30%, considerably narrowing the gap between these two modes.

Cycling represented 10% of commuting journeys at the start of the period, the same proportion as walking. Ten years later, the bicycle figure had doubled to 20%, whereas walking remained unchanged at 10%. Together, cycling and walking accounted for 30% of journeys in 2020, compared with 20% in 2010.

title: Investing in public transport
prompt: Some people believe governments should spend more money improving public transport than building new roads. To what extent do you agree or disagree? Give reasons for your answer and include relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience. Write at least 250 words.
planningTips: Choose a clear degree of agreement; you can support public transport while allowing necessary road maintenance.
Develop one reason per body paragraph, such as moving more people efficiently and improving access to work.
Explain why your example supports the argument; avoid making up research statistics.
Address a limitation briefly, such as areas too sparsely populated for frequent buses.
sampleAnswer:
Governments must balance growing travel demand with limited public funds. I largely agree that improving public transport should receive greater priority than building new roads, particularly in cities. However, this should not prevent essential road maintenance or carefully chosen improvements in remote areas.

The main reason to favour public transport is that it can move large numbers of people while using relatively little road space. A frequent bus service may offer a practical alternative to driving, especially when dedicated lanes make journey times predictable. In contrast, an additional road does not necessarily solve congestion if it encourages more people to travel by car. Investment should therefore focus on complete journeys: reliable services are more useful when passengers can also reach stops safely and change between routes easily.

Better public transport can also widen access to work and education. People who cannot afford a car still need to travel to jobs, colleges and medical appointments. If services are infrequent or stop early in the evening, those people may have to reject opportunities that are otherwise suitable. For example, an affordable bus connecting an outer neighbourhood with a hospital could benefit both patients and staff working different shifts. Such an improvement has a value that extends beyond reducing traffic.

Nevertheless, transport needs differ between places. In a sparsely populated district, maintaining a safe road may serve residents more effectively than running frequent buses with very few passengers. Emergency services and deliveries also depend on usable roads. These needs justify targeted spending, even when public transport receives the larger share of a city's investment.

In conclusion, governments should generally prioritise reliable and accessible public transport because of its capacity and social benefits. Road spending remains necessary, but new construction should respond to a clear local need rather than be treated as the automatic answer to congestion.

title: Practical skills and academic subjects
prompt: Some people think schools should focus on academic subjects, while others believe practical life skills are equally important. Discuss both views and give your own opinion. Write at least 250 words.
planningTips: Discuss the reasons behind both views rather than simply naming them.
State your own view clearly in the introduction and conclusion.
Show how practical skills can complement academic learning.
Use specific examples, such as evaluating a household budget, instead of broad claims that a subject is useful.
sampleAnswer:
Schools have limited teaching time, so deciding what belongs in the curriculum involves difficult choices. Some people favour a strong focus on academic subjects, while others want practical life skills to receive equal attention. In my view, academic learning should remain central, but schools should also provide structured opportunities to apply it to everyday responsibilities.

Those who prioritise academic subjects argue that schools have a particular responsibility to develop knowledge that students may struggle to acquire elsewhere. Mathematics, science and history introduce systematic ways of thinking, and they provide foundations for further study. A pupil who lacks basic mathematical understanding may find later technical training difficult, regardless of how confident they are with everyday tasks. Moreover, reducing teaching time too far could disadvantage students whose families cannot afford additional tuition.

The case for practical skills is also strong. Young adults must manage money, understand information about health and communicate in unfamiliar situations. These abilities are not acquired automatically when a student passes an examination. For instance, someone may be able to perform calculations but still need help comparing the total cost of two payment plans. Schools can provide a consistent starting point, especially for children who have few opportunities to discuss such matters at home.

I believe the most effective approach is to connect these aims wherever possible. A mathematics lesson could include planning a realistic budget, while a language course could teach students to write a clear formal request. Some topics may require separate sessions, but practical learning need not displace entire academic subjects. Teachers would need appropriate resources so that these activities deepen understanding rather than become superficial additions.

In conclusion, academic subjects offer essential intellectual foundations, and practical skills help students use those foundations beyond school. A balanced curriculum should protect academic depth while giving all pupils meaningful practice with the responsibilities they will encounter as adults.

My own opinion is clear throughout.

title: Working from home
prompt: More employers now allow staff to work from home. Do the advantages of this development outweigh the disadvantages? Give reasons and relevant examples. Write at least 250 words.
planningTips: Make an explicit judgement about which side outweighs the other.
Explain how benefits depend on the type of work.
Develop a disadvantage rather than dismissing it.
sampleAnswer:
Working from home has become an option in many occupations where tasks can be completed digitally. Although this arrangement can weaken informal communication, I believe its advantages generally outweigh its disadvantages when employers establish suitable routines and preserve opportunities for direct contact.

The main benefit is the greater control employees gain over time that would otherwise be spent commuting. Someone who previously travelled for an hour each way can use part of that time for rest, exercise or family responsibilities. This does not mean that working hours should become shorter without agreement. Rather, it removes an activity that consumes time without directly contributing to the employee's work. Employers may also recruit from a wider area when attendance at an office is not required every day.

There are nevertheless real disadvantages. A new employee may find it difficult to ask small questions when colleagues are available only through scheduled calls. At home, unsuitable space or competing responsibilities can also make concentration difficult. These problems are especially important for people who share crowded accommodation. It would therefore be unfair to assume that every employee has the same capacity to work effectively outside the office.

In my view, these limitations call for flexibility rather than the rejection of remote work. Teams can arrange regular check-ins and agree which activities benefit most from meeting in person. An employer could also retain shared workspaces for those who need them. Such arrangements preserve the time-saving benefit while reducing isolation and ensuring that location does not become a barrier to receiving support.

In conclusion, the advantages of working from home are greater overall because it reduces unnecessary travel and broadens employment options. However, this judgement depends on providing appropriate support and recognising that a single arrangement will not suit every worker or task.

title: Reducing household food waste
prompt: Many households throw away food that could have been eaten. What problems does this cause, and what measures could reduce it? Give reasons and relevant examples. Write at least 250 words.
planningTips: Discuss consequences, not only causes.

sampleAnswer:
Edible food is sometimes discarded because households buy more than they use or forget what they already have. This creates financial and environmental problems. A combination of clearer information, practical household routines and suitable retail options could reduce the amount thrown away.

One problem is that wasted food represents wasted household income. Families pay for products from which they receive no nutritional benefit, and repeated small losses can place pressure on a limited budget. There is also a wider waste of resources. Producing, transporting and storing food require land, water, energy and labour. When usable food is discarded, these inputs have been used without fulfilling their purpose. The issue therefore extends beyond the rubbish visible in a kitchen bin.

At household level, planning meals and checking existing supplies before shopping can reduce unnecessary purchases. A family that knows which vegetables are already in its refrigerator is less likely to buy duplicates. Storing food appropriately and using older items first can also help. These routines need to be simple enough to maintain; a complicated recording system would be unlikely to suit a busy household.

Retailers and public organisations have a role as well. Shops could offer practical pack sizes instead of making large quantities the only economical option. Clear explanations of food labels would help consumers understand the information available to them, while community cooking sessions could demonstrate ways of using suitable leftovers. Such measures address knowledge and purchasing conditions rather than placing all responsibility on individual willpower.

In conclusion, throwing away edible food wastes money and the resources invested in its production. Better planning, clear information and more flexible purchasing options can work together to reduce this problem, even though some waste will remain unavoidable.

title: Moving to larger cities
prompt: Many young adults move from small towns to large cities. Why do they make this move? How can smaller towns encourage them to stay? Give reasons and relevant examples. Write at least 250 words.
planningTips: Answer both questions with balanced development.
Connect the town measures to the reasons for moving.
Avoid treating all young adults as having identical priorities.
sampleAnswer:
For many young adults, moving to a large city seems a useful step towards independence. Employment and educational opportunities are major reasons for this decision. Smaller towns are more likely to retain young residents if they improve access to these opportunities while preserving the advantages of local life.

Large cities tend to offer a wider choice of employers and courses within a relatively small area. A young person seeking specialist training may have few suitable options in their home town. Similarly, someone entering a creative or technical field may value living near several potential employers rather than depending on a single local firm. Cities can also offer social and cultural opportunities that appeal to people establishing new friendships. However, the importance of these attractions will differ between individuals.

Smaller towns can respond by strengthening links between education and local employment. Colleges could work with businesses to provide relevant training and placements, allowing students to see a future career without immediately moving away. Reliable digital connections can also make some remote jobs practical. These measures are more useful than simply promoting the town's scenery if the main reason for leaving is the absence of suitable work.

The quality of everyday life matters too. Affordable housing, dependable transport and welcoming spaces for recreation can make staying attractive. For example, a shared workspace near a bus route could help young remote workers avoid isolation while remaining close to family. Town authorities should consult young residents when choosing such projects so that investment reflects their actual needs rather than assumptions made on their behalf.

In conclusion, young adults often move to cities for broader study, career and social possibilities. Smaller towns can encourage them to stay by making local opportunities more credible and supporting an enjoyable, connected daily life.

title: A shift towards digital payments
prompt: In some communities, people increasingly use digital payments instead of cash. Is this a positive or negative development? Give reasons and relevant examples. Write at least 250 words.
planningTips: Give an overall evaluation, not just a list of pros and cons.
Consider people who may be excluded.
Support practical claims with examples rather than invented statistics.
sampleAnswer:
Digital payments are replacing cash in many everyday transactions. I regard this as a largely positive development because it can make payments more convenient and easier to track. However, maintaining alternatives is important so that people without suitable devices or skills are not excluded.

The main advantage is convenience. A customer can pay a bill or purchase a service without first obtaining the exact amount of cash. For a small business, an electronic record may also make it easier to check which payments have been received. Consider a local class that accepts advance payments: a clear transaction record can reduce misunderstandings about whether a place has been paid for. These benefits concern both the speed of the transaction and the information available afterward.

Nevertheless, digital payments are not equally accessible to everyone. Some people lack reliable connectivity, while others may find unfamiliar interfaces difficult to use. Technical interruptions can also prevent a transaction even when both parties are willing to proceed. If essential services refuse every alternative, a convenient system for most customers can become a barrier for a minority. Concerns about personal information and fraudulent requests make clear guidance important as well.

These limitations do not make the wider change negative, but they should shape how it is introduced. Businesses can offer assistance, use straightforward payment procedures and keep an appropriate alternative for customers who need one. Public information should explain how to recognise legitimate requests without assuming advanced technical knowledge. The aim should be to expand people's choices rather than require everyone to adopt the same method immediately.

In conclusion, greater use of digital payments is positive when convenience and clearer records are accompanied by inclusive access. The benefits are strongest when communities preserve practical alternatives and help users understand the system.
